title: Two Phosphate Switches That Flip Waiting Factors

scenes.visual: Title card 'Two Phosphate Switches That Flip Waiting Factors' fades over the carried 2D cell cross-section (filling 70% of frame): slate-blue plasma membrane arc on left, warm dark cytosol center, dashed nuclear envelope opening into deep-indigo nucleus at right with a bright white horizontal DNA bar along the bottom-right. Shared colour map for both films: amber-gold phosphate dots (#F59E0B), coral-orange cAMP/PKA (#FB7185), cyan-teal calcium/CaMKIV/calcineurin (#22D3EE), violet-purple CREB (#A78BFA), emerald-green CBP (#34D399), sky-blue NFAT (#38BDF8) with lime-green entry badge (#84CC16), crimson drug clamp (#EF4444), mint mRNA ribbon (#6EE7B7).

scenes.tts: How can a resting cell switch on a gene in minutes, even with every ribosome stopped? Add a growth factor, and C fos transcripts still surge. Whatever switched the gene on was already built and waiting. The signal only had to flip it.
scenes.caption: How can a resting cell switch on a gene in minutes, even with every ribosome stopped? Add a growth factor, and c-fos transcripts still surge. Whatever switched the gene on was already built and waiting. The signal only had to flip it.
scenes.visual: A glowing signal pulse strikes a receptor on the slate-blue plasma membrane while a crossed-out ribosome icon pulses in the cytosol ('Ribosomes stopped'). Inside the nucleus, a bright mint mRNA ribbon labelled 'c-fos mRNA' streams off the white DNA bar. A bold question overlay reads 'What was waiting?'.
scenes.narration: How can a resting cell switch on a gene in minutes, even with every ribosome stopped? Add a growth factor, and c-fos transcripts still surge. Whatever switched the gene on was already built and waiting. The signal only had to flip it.

scenes.tts: A transcription factor binds a short DNA site near a gene. Making a new factor is slow, since it must be transcribed and translated. Fast pathways modify a factor already made. One waiting factor is Creb. It sits on DNA as a pair before any signal arrives, yet stays quiet.
scenes.caption: A transcription factor binds a short DNA site near a gene. Making a new factor is slow, since it must be transcribed and translated. Fast pathways modify a factor already made. One waiting factor is CREB. It sits on DNA as a pair before any signal arrives, yet stays quiet.
scenes.visual: Camera zooms smoothly into the deep-indigo nucleus, keeping the nuclear envelope visible on the left. Two paired violet blocks labelled 'CREB' sit parked on a glowing white DNA slot labelled 'CRE'. Subtle ambient shimmer on DNA; RNA polymerase remains dim and unattached nearby to show the gene is still off.
scenes.narration: A transcription factor binds a short DNA site near a gene. Making a new factor is slow, since it must be transcribed and translated. Fast pathways modify a factor already made. One waiting factor is CREB. It sits on DNA as a pair before any signal arrives, yet stays quiet.

scenes.tts: When cyclic A M P rises, it frees the active subunits of P K A. Some enter the nucleus and attach one phosphate onto Creb at serine one thirty-three. That phosphate is a docking handle. C B P, a co-activator that cannot bind DNA itself, grips it through its Kix pocket. C B P then adds acetyl groups that loosen packaged DNA and calls in RNA polymerase.
scenes.caption: When cyclic AMP rises, it frees the active subunits of PKA. Some enter the nucleus and attach one phosphate onto CREB at serine 133. That phosphate is a docking handle. CBP, a co-activator that cannot bind DNA itself, grips it through its KIX pocket. CBP then adds acetyl groups that loosen packaged DNA and calls in RNA polymerase.
scenes.visual: Coral-orange dots ('cAMP') rise in the cytosol and release coral 'PKA' blocks that glide through a nuclear pore. PKA snaps a bright amber-gold 'P' circle ('Ser 133') onto violet CREB. An emerald-green crescent labelled 'CBP (KIX)' docks snugly onto the 'P' handle, gently uncoiling schematic histone spools on the DNA as a glowing RNA polymerase block lands and starts a mint mRNA ribbon.
scenes.narration: When cyclic AMP rises, it frees the active subunits of PKA. Some enter the nucleus and attach one phosphate onto CREB at serine 133. That phosphate is a docking handle. CBP, a co-activator that cannot bind DNA itself, grips it through its KIX pocket. CBP then adds acetyl groups that loosen packaged DNA and calls in RNA polymerase.

scenes.tts: Next, a different messenger: calcium. Calcium binds calmodulin, and the pair switches on a nuclear kinase, Cam kinase four. It puts a phosphate onto the exact same serine of Creb. Growth factors reach that serine too, through kinases that E R K switches on. So separate signals flip one switch.
scenes.caption: Next, a different messenger: calcium. Calcium binds calmodulin, and the pair switches on a nuclear kinase, CaMKIV. It puts a phosphate onto the exact same serine of CREB. Growth factors reach that serine too, through kinases that ERK switches on. So separate signals flip one switch.
scenes.visual: Reset the amber 'P' off CREB while holding the same nuclear view. Cyan-teal dots ('Ca2+') stream through a membrane channel on the left, join a cyan 'CaM' ring, and light up a nuclear cyan block ('CaMKIV'). CaMKIV snaps the exact same amber 'P' onto CREB Ser 133; a faint secondary arrow labelled 'kinases ERK switches on' also points to the same 'P' spot, and emerald CBP docks again.
scenes.narration: Next, a different messenger: calcium. Calcium binds calmodulin, and the pair switches on a nuclear kinase, CaMKIV. It puts a phosphate onto the exact same serine of CREB. Growth factors reach that serine too, through kinases that ERK switches on. So separate signals flip one switch.

scenes.tts: Adding a phosphate is one switch. Meet a second pre-made factor, N F A T, resting in the cytoplasm. It carries about a dozen phosphates that cover its nuclear entry tag. Here, removing phosphates activates the factor, because those phosphates were locking it outside.
scenes.caption: Adding a phosphate is one switch. Meet a second pre-made factor, NFAT, resting in the cytoplasm. It carries about a dozen phosphates that cover its nuclear entry tag. Here, removing phosphates activates the factor, because those phosphates were locking it outside.
scenes.visual: Pan back out to the full cell cross-section so both cytosol and nucleus fill the frame. In the cytosol floats a large sky-blue block labelled 'NFAT', ringed by a cluster of amber-gold 'P' circles physically masking a glowing lime-green badge labelled 'Import tag'. A gentle bounce against the nuclear envelope shows NFAT cannot cross while covered.
scenes.narration: Adding a phosphate is one switch. Meet a second pre-made factor, NFAT, resting in the cytoplasm. It carries about a dozen phosphates that cover its nuclear entry tag. Here, removing phosphates activates the factor, because those phosphates were locking it outside.

scenes.tts: When the T cell receptor fires, sustained calcium turns on calcineurin, a phosphatase that removes phosphates. Pause and predict: once those phosphates come off, where does this factor go?
scenes.caption: When the T cell receptor fires, sustained calcium turns on calcineurin, a phosphatase that removes phosphates. Pause and predict: once those phosphates come off, where does this factor go?
scenes.visual: Cyan-teal 'Ca2+' pours in steadily at the left membrane and lights up a cyan crescent labelled 'Calcineurin' approaching the sky-blue NFAT block. A clean high-contrast prompt card slides above: 'Calcineurin removes phosphates -> Where does NFAT go?'.
scenes.narration: When the T cell receptor fires, sustained calcium turns on calcineurin, a phosphatase that removes phosphates. Pause and predict: once those phosphates come off, where does this factor go?

scenes.visual: Thinking pause: keep the question card and the scene of cyan calcineurin hovering beside phosphorylated sky-blue NFAT on screen. A thin glowing progress bar slowly sweeps beneath the question while the amber 'P' dots shimmer gently.

scenes.tts: The factor moves into the nucleus, because calcineurin strips the phosphates that covered its entry tag. With the tag exposed, it glides through a pore and switches on target genes. When calcium drops, kinases restore those phosphates and send it back out.
scenes.caption: The factor moves into the nucleus, because calcineurin strips the phosphates that covered its entry tag. With the tag exposed, it glides through a pore and switches on target genes. When calcium drops, kinases restore those phosphates and send it back out.
scenes.visual: Question card clears. Cyan calcineurin sweeps past NFAT, popping the amber 'P' dots away; the lime-green 'Import tag' flares bright and sky-blue NFAT glides smoothly through a nuclear pore onto the white DNA bar. Then cyan Ca2+ fades, small kinase chevrons reattach amber 'P' dots, and NFAT exits back into the cytosol.
scenes.narration: The factor moves into the nucleus, because calcineurin strips the phosphates that covered its entry tag. With the tag exposed, it glides through a pore and switches on target genes. When calcium drops, kinases restore those phosphates and send it back out.

scenes.tts: Two transplant drugs, cyclosporin A and F K five oh six, quiet T cells by jamming this switch. Neither drug blocks calcineurin on its own. Each binds a small helper protein. That pair sits beside calcineurin's active site and keeps protein substrates from reaching it.
scenes.caption: Two transplant drugs, cyclosporin A and FK506, quiet T cells by jamming this switch. Neither drug blocks calcineurin on its own. Each binds a small helper protein. That pair sits beside calcineurin's active site and keeps protein substrates from reaching it.
scenes.visual: In the cytosol, a crimson pill ('Drug') snaps onto a crimson helper wedge ('Helper protein') to form a clamp. The clamp docks right beside the active notch of cyan calcineurin (not inside the notch), and a generic grey substrate block ('Protein substrate') bumps against the clamp and cannot reach the notch.
scenes.narration: Two transplant drugs, cyclosporin A and FK506, quiet T cells by jamming this switch. Neither drug blocks calcineurin on its own. Each binds a small helper protein. That pair sits beside calcineurin's active site and keeps protein substrates from reaching it.

scenes.tts: Back to the opening puzzle. Whether a signal adds one phosphate or removes many, the protein was built in advance. Fast signals flip pre-made factors to switch on first-wave genes like C fos within minutes. Stopped ribosomes cannot stop a waiting switch.

scenes.visual: The frame widens to show both switches active side by side in the carried cell—violet CREB on DNA gaining one amber 'P' and sky-blue NFAT losing phosphates to enter—while bright mint 'c-fos mRNA' streams off DNA beside the crossed-out ribosome icon.
